Hi8mV09nOi.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLN-CE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over both baselines beyond simulation.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

The framework is trained with dense sector flow field supervision and evaluated on a Habitat-based benchmark built from R2R/RxR episodes and zero-shot real-world closed-loop execution.

G6vrRbO3NE.abstract: Driver alerting from dashcam video is a sequential decision problem under partial observability: a system must warn early enough to support driver response, while avoiding frequent nuisance alerts. Existing approaches often reduce this problem to binary risk prediction, forcing a thresholded silent-or-alert decision even when visual evidence is incomplete. We propose VLAlert, a vision-language framework that formulates driver alerting as a tri-action policy over Silent, Observe, and Alert. The Observe action serves as an internal evidence-gathering state, allowing the system to defer uncertain warnings and adapt its subsequent observation window before issuing a driver-facing alert. VLAlert adapts a 4B vision-language model to generate structured safety-evidence spans and uses hidden states pooled from these spans as compact belief representations for danger estimation and policy prediction. To evaluate alerting beyond threshold-free anticipation metrics, we construct VLAlert-Bench, a unified per-tick benchmark from multiple driving-alert datasets, and introduce DAUS, a driver-aware utility score that jointly measures ranking, video coverage, false-alert burden, and lead-time utility. Experiments show that VLAlert achieves the best overall operating-point utility among representative video and VLM baselines. Ablations further indicate that structured belief-span pooling improves alert separability and that retaining Observe as a separate action provides useful supervision for uncertain pre-alert states.
keywords: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems

JydY4anB01.abstract:
Embodied Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning modules in robotic control pipelines to improve human-robot interaction, but their memory and generation latency make real-time deployment difficult. Pruning can reduce these costs, but for controllers that undergo multiple pre- and post-training phases, the crucial question is not only how much to prune, but when pruning should occur.

In this work, we propose Before Parc Fermé (BPF), a pruning strategy performed during RL that compresses embodied LLM controllers while they are still being optimized for closed-loop behavior. This allows pruning decisions to account for the task-specific supervision and closed-loop feedback that shape the final controller. We propose two variants: BPF-RL, which performs iterative pruning during RL by removing part of the model at predefined training intervals, and BPF-SFT/RL, which first prunes part of the model structure during SFT and then further compresses it during RL using the same iterative strategy as BPF-RL until the target pruning ratio is reached.
We evaluate BPF on RobotxR1, an LLM-based autonomous-driving control pipeline, using an established LLM pruning framework (LLM-Pruner), and compare it against post-training pruning, post-training pruning with RL recovery, SFT-stage pruning, and smaller dense models from the same family.

Our results show that BPF provides the best task-performance vs. memory and throughput trade-off among the considered pruning strategies. When compressing the larger RobotxR1 models, BPF-SFT/RL achieves a $1.69\times$ better size-end-to-end performance trade-off than directly selecting a smaller dense model from the same family, measured as removed parameters per lost percentage point of control adaptability. On the Jetson AGX Orin mounted on the target robotic platform, the compact models improve decode throughput by up to $27\%$. Finally,we further show that pruning must be evaluated end-to-end, since changes in generated output tokens can affect downstream latency and closed-loop behavior.
keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

oMvcKDFLRA.abstract: Generating safety-critical scenarios is essential for validating and improving autonomous driving systems, yet it inherently requires maximizing adversariality to expose failures while preserving realism. Existing methods usually manage this trade-off with handcrafted heuristics, confining generation to known priors and overlooking underexplored patterns. While recent open-ended agentic evolution can push this limit, unconstrained general agents lack strict simulator grounding and tend to collapse the multi-objective tension into single-scalar maximization. Here we present EvoDrive, the first automated, LLM-based agentic evolution framework for multi-objective scenario generation. EvoDrive employs a simulator-grounded actor-critic architecture where a memory-driven actor iteratively proposes improvements to the generators and critics filter out implausible candidates, and a self-evolving world evaluator routes promising proposals to optimize simulation budgets. EvoDrive further maintains a Pareto archive of evaluated candidates to preserve diverse attack-realism trade-offs and guide future evolution via simulation feedback. Benchmark results on MetaDrive and CARLA show that EvoDrive not only significantly expands the Pareto frontier across various generators, but also produces valuable scenarios for policy training.
keywords: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming

eGZ6YMFVzU.abstract: Anomaly detection is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of autonomous driving systems operating in open environments, where rare objects, abnormal behaviors, and long-tail events frequently arise. Conventional perception-based approaches often lack the contextual understanding necessary to interpret complex anomalies, while recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods incur substantial computational overhead and exhibit limited integration with geometric sensory modalities. To address these challenges, we propose SOFA, an adaptive slow-fast anomaly detection and reasoning framework that selectively activates multimodal reasoning only when anomalous events are detected. SOFA integrates three key components: 1) a fast LiDAR-based anomaly detection module for efficient real-time perception, 2) a slow VLM-based reasoning module for semantic understanding, and 3) a Time-to-Collision (TTC)-driven switching mechanism that dynamically coordinates the two modules to balance efficiency and reasoning fidelity. To enable systematic evaluation of multimodal anomaly detection and reasoning in real-world driving scenarios, we further construct MAQA, a Multimodal Anomaly Question Answering dataset comprising 16K anomalous objects, synchronized LiDAR-image observations, and reasoning-oriented language annotations. Extensive experiments on MAQA demonstrate that SOFA significantly outperforms baselines in detection accuracy, computational efficiency, and reasoning capability.
keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning

022K2ZIPR6.abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. This insight reveals that instead of complex over-engineering, general VLMs merely require a targeted geometric catalyst to bridge the spatial gap. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

sdujBb3P4e.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise to bring end-to-end reasoning to autonomous driving, but their computational cost is orders of magnitude too high for real-time control. The core challenge is that VLA inference is not a single bottleneck but a pipeline of four stages (visual encoding, language model prefilling, reasoning-token decoding, and flow-matching action prediction), each dominated by a different source of inefficiency: spatial redundancy in overlapping video frames, autoregressive serialization of reasoning chains, and over-computation in iterative denoising. Addressing any one stage in isolation leaves the others untouched.
We propose FlashDrive, an algorithm-system co-design framework that targets all four stages simultaneously. A key insight is that each bottleneck admits a distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcut: temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames; the low entropy of domain-specific reasoning tokens makes them amenable to diffusion-based speculative decoding; and the non-uniform structure of the denoising velocity field, sharp at the endpoints but nearly constant in the middle, permits adaptive step caching that concentrates compute where it matters. Layered on top of system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion, these techniques compound multiplicatively. Applied to Alpamayo1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization, \method reduces end-to-end latency from 716~ms to 159~ms (4.5x) with negligible accuracy loss (~0.07m on minADE6@6.4s and ADE@6.4s even improves), bringing VLA-driven autonomous driving to real-time viability on consumer-level GPUs.

FlashDrive achieves a 4.7 × 4.7\times latency reduction (down to 151 ms) while incurring negligible degradation on minADE 6 \text{minADE}_{6} @6.4s and even improving minADE 1 \text{minADE}_{1} @6.4s.

vVIVf2E7KG.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly-simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach exploits this spatial structure; at each step, we query the BEV features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally provide a benchmarking approach to extensively evaluate dynamics models on challenging datasets collected across all seasons, decreasing the worst-case prediction accuracy by 23.8\%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 34.9\% reduction in maximum cross-track error.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

Alu9eLT93i.abstract: Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student–teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which distills a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher's behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

msKuD5tWYj.abstract: Learning a single policy that reaches a goal with high geometric precision while interacting safely with nearby agents poses conflicting objectives. Precision favors commitment to a fixed geometric plan, whereas interaction requires immediate deviation when another agent intrudes, causing policies optimized for one objective to often fail at the other. We study this problem in the context of reactive autonomous parking, where multiple vehicles must reach assigned slots with sub-meter terminal accuracy while remaining responsive to neighboring vehicles throughout the maneuver. We propose CoPark, a self-play RL approach that learns reactive parking through multi-agent self-play, built on a residual-policy architecture. A precomputed offline plan provides a fixed action prior, while a residual head learns the reactive corrections. This decomposition separates geometric consistency from interaction. The residual policy learns behaviors under self-play, where data and scripting fall short, while the fixed prior holds the slot-frame geometry that pure policies struggle to reach reliably. The key design is a partner-threat-modulated, channel-asymmetric release of the prior. A continuous threat signal shifts authority of the longitudinal channel to the residual head to enable yielding, while the lateral channel remains anchored to the precomputed reference to preserve sub-meter slot alignment. A closed-loop refinement layer corrects residual terminal error from action-grid discretization. We train our policy on six parking lots and evaluate zero-shot on our new reactive-parking benchmark spanning Dragon Lake Parking (DLP) and DeepScenario Open 3D (DSC3D). CoPark achieves ~70-85% success with only 3-6% collision rate, substantially outperforming classical, imitation-learning, and large-scale RL baselines. Importantly, the results demonstrate emergent interaction behaviors such as reverse-yielding, mid-maneuver yielding, tight-corridor passing, and queuing.
keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics

4RLjGPEfpH.abstract: Zero-shot generalization to unseen embodiments is important for generalizable vision-language-action (VLA) models as robot hardware evolves and task-specific data collection remains costly. However, a systematic understanding of this problem remains limited, in part because the literature lacks a unified zero-shot transfer definition and controlled evaluation settings that isolate embodiment changes from differences in tasks, scenes, or protocols. To address this gap, we first distinguishstrict zero-shot transfer, where the target embodiment is absent from all training data, from pretrain-exposed zero-shot transfer, where it appears only during pretraining. We then introduce a controlled benchmark spanning 14 held-out target embodiments across simulation and real-world validation. Within this framework, we systematically study four factors: state-action representations, pretraining embodiment diversity, auxiliary co-training objectives, and target-embodiment exposure. Experimental results show that local end-effector (EEF) state-action representations, the source-diversity comparison, and auxiliary co-training improve cross-embodiment transfer by around 15, 18, and 7 percentage points, respectively. We further find that adding only 5\% target-embodiment data during pretraining improves average target-embodiment progress by 13.4 percentage points, showing that strict and pretrain-exposed zero-shot transfer are distinct and should be reported separately. Together, these findings provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving cross-embodiment VLA transfer.
keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Learning representations for robotic perception and control

FVZKpmPHV8.abstract: VLA models are conditioned on a single observation at inference time, a design that suffices for quasi-static manipulation but creates two representational failures in dynamic settings. The first is motion ambiguity: a snapshot encodes configuration, not how the scene is evolving, so the policy cannot anticipate where a moving target will be. The second is state aliasing: perceptually similar observations at different task phases can demand opposite actions, producing jitter and mistimed commitments even on tasks the policy nominally understands. We show that these two failures are separable and that each has a natural fix: a motion summary from a frozen video foundation model separates scene dynamics from appearance without task-specific supervision, while a compact proprioceptive history disambiguates sequential task phases without per-task engineering. TEMPO adds these as minimal inputs to a pretrained VLA without architectural modification. On four dynamic bimanual tasks, TEMPO improves Bottle Handover success from 44% to 74% and is the only system to succeed on tasks where state-of-the-art asynchronous baselines score 0% due to unresolved state aliasing. Probing and ablation analyses confirm that each signal is individually necessary, suggesting that what limits VLAs in dynamic settings is not model capacity but the right temporal context.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

nXfwmrzXzz.abstract:
Proactive robot assistance requires acting on user needs before explicit requests, but zero-shot vision-language models struggle in this setting: lacking knowledge of the user's personal routine, they treat every situation as general and uncertain, defaulting to inaction rather than risking an incorrect intervention. We observe that everyday routines are highly repetitive, so even a few interactions
reveal stable user-specific patterns that can ground proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a System 1--2 framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a \emph{Procedural Assistance Memory} (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when and how to assist, and a VLA executor realizes the predicted task as low-level robot action. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. We evaluate on a multi-day desk-assistance scenario with six pick-and-place tasks. Memory-free baselines remain conservative across all five evaluation days, yielding near-zero recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds
on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Ablations further show that the FSM structure, rather than memory alone, is the primary driver of these gains.
keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction

AAn8ouEHwO.abstract: Reinforcement learning for robot manipulation is bottlenecked by reward design: hand-crafted rewards are brittle and prohibitively task-specific, while learned reward models typically demand additional task data and handle failures poorly, leaving them vulnerable to reward hacking. To address this, we introduce the Reference-Anchored Reward Model (RARM), a lightweight visual comparator that leverages a single reference demonstration to generate dense, progress-aware rewards with no per-task reward engineering. RARM couples a DINOv3 backbone with low-rank adapters, a temporal aggregator, and an asymmetric cross-attention comparator, trained once with a contrastive objective on ordinary videos and requiring no robot-specific data. At policy-training time, each rollout clip is matched against reference clips from the demonstration, and the reward is based on confidence-gated progress change from the matched clip, anchoring learning to that single demonstration. Across 10 simulated tasks (LIBERO, MetaWorld) and 4 real-world tasks, including long-horizon settings, RARM achieves the best overall success rates while adding negligible per-step reward generation overhead.
keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

jnEHLRyWTZ.abstract:
Behavior cloning for robot manipulation is based on expert demonstration datasets. However, for tasks that require dynamic
stability, precise contact timing, or dexterous coordination, human teleoperators may find it hard or even impossible to collect data. We study this infeasible-demonstration regime and propose GLIDE, a framework that infers task-specific failure points and converts them into executable guardrails for data collection and policy deployment. Given a task description, GLIDE writes guardrails that use robot state to filter teleoperation and policy commands, constrain failure-prone actions, and iteratively improve from closed-loop dataset feedback. Across Tomato plate transfer, Marker handover & stand, and Wine serving tasks, GLIDE improves data collection efficiency over raw VR
teleoperation and manually designed guardrails. After refinement, GLIDE raises data-collection efficiency from 0-10% to 70-90% across the three tasks. During policy execution, guarded deployment raises Tomato plate transfer policy success from 0% to 60-70%, enabling efficient learning on mixed-quality demonstrations. These results show that GLIDE guardrails can support policy learning when direct demonstrations are unreliable.
keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction

8xaYRUduNe.abstract: Control-space tree search sidesteps the steering requirement of geometric search methods and offers an asymptotic route to natively feasible kinodynamic trajectories. In practice, however, control-space search fails on the simplest of motion-planning instances for nonlinear systems such as quadrotors. This failure is rooted in poor geometric coverage induced when naive control-sampling measures are pushed forward through system dynamics. We resolve this problem by learning a lightweight sampler whose pushforward achieves low geometric dispersion in the local search space. The central idea is to utilize a well-dispersed reference map as a training scaffold, eliminating the need for an external expert. Our experiments then demonstrate that the learned sampler enables control-space search for quadrotor motion planning when naive sampling measures simply fail. Once enabled, control-space planning is shown to generate highly agile trajectory solutions in an obstacle-dense setting as compared to established trajectory optimization techniques. We also show that the geometric reach of the learned model dominates popular motion primitive libraries, spanning roughly thrice their volume. Arbitrarily low-dispersion primitives are thus made available for any state merely by scaling test-time compute.
keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics

WNZ4Dr57JS.abstract: Tremendous progress has been made toward zero-shot, 3D-object-prompted perception tasks, including detection, segmentation, and 6D pose estimation. However, prior methods still struggle to see widespread use in robotics due to complexities such as challenging materials, dense clutter, and runtime. To address these limitations, we introduce Z3P, the first competitive end-to-end transformer architecture that performs zero-shot detection, segmentation, and pose estimation from single/multi-view RGB or RGB-D data and a 3D-object prompt. While previous methods use bounding boxes as an intermediate step between multiple models, Z3P operates as a single network that maintains an internal representation through persistent object tokens, allowing for better runtime and improved performance in densely cluttered environments with challenging materials. Across five robotic benchmarks (IPD, XYZ-IBD, ITODD-MV, T-ROBI, and ROBI), Z3P establishes a new state-of-the-art by becoming the first zero-shot method to outperform all prior zero-shot and object-specific approaches on detection and pose estimation. Finally, we demonstrate Z3P's utility as a foundation model for 3D-object perception, generalizing to multiple demanding robotic applications, including transparent object bin picking, sorting, car charging, and electronics assembly.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision
Learning representations for robotic perception and control

awVlNORXDS.abstract:
Neural inertial odometry has demonstrated strong potential for motion estimation in challenging environments, yet inertial-only preintegration remains sensitive to IMU bias and uncertainty.
To this end, this paper introduces \textbf{PLATO}:~\emph{Privileged Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations}, a likelihood-based framework that leverages accurate trajectory observations to jointly learn IMU bias dynamics modeled by a neural ordinary differential equation~(NODE) and gyroscope and accelerometer noise covariances.
Optimization exploits the sparse structure of the negative log-likelihood, with IMU noise-parameter gradients computed by forward differentiation.
A tailored double-adjoint scheme couples a discrete invariant-error adjoint with a continuous-time adjoint for the bias NODE, enabling memory-efficient likelihood optimization over the nested bias-dynamics and IMU-preintegration rollouts.
Validation on EuRoC shows improved performance, and underwater robot experiments demonstrate applicability under intermittent lighting failures and visual degradation.
keywords: Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics
Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

w3g5PWur7i.abstract: Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and continuous policy evolution. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable \textit{atomic skills}. It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference. Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations. Evaluations across the simulated BEHAVIOR-1K benchmark and real-world tasks demonstrate that MobiAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art monolithic VLAs, achieving a +22.5% higher success rate in simulation. Furthermore, it demonstrates robust error recovery against critical failures and enables steady, annotation-free policy evolution via autonomous data recycling.
keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics
Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

The rollout trace illustrates a failed placement where the can drops outside the trash. In response, MobiAgent triggers replanning, guiding the robot to approach the displaced can, re-grasp it, and complete the task. uizBY3yrgz.abstract:
The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike the large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection is an active process incurring prohibitive physical costs. As a result, the key challenge is not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain training data that provides informative learning knowledge by broadening behavioral coverage and capturing meaningful variations in objects, scenes, and skills. However, how to automatically curate task proposals that maximize the utility of collected robot data remains a critical yet under-explored challenge.

To address this, we introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework designed to automate the generation of diverse and informative manipulation tasks across heterogeneous robotic embodiments, spanning single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene integrates three core components: (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement. We conduct extensive quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, collecting datasets of 18k trajectories and introducing novel metrics to assess task quality in terms of feasibility and diversity. Results demonstrate that RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Furthermore, real-world experiments show that VLA models trained on data generated by RoboGene achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the importance of high-quality task generation. Our project is available at https://x-robogene.github.io/.

2dEfANeQL7.abstract: Scaling humanoid loco-manipulation requires robot-compatible demonstrations across diverse objects, whole-body motions, and scene geometries, but teleoperation and motion capture are difficult to scale because each collection depends on physical setups, instrumented actors, and robot operation. We present GRAIL, a digital generation pipeline that remains fully virtual until deployment: it composes 3D assets, simulator-ready scenes, and priors from video foundation models (VFMs) to synthesize interactions without rebuilding physical environments or teleoperating the robot. Rather than reconstructing unconstrained in-the-wild videos, GRAIL starts from fully specified 3D configurations in which object geometry, camera parameters, metric scale, environment depth, and a robot-proportioned character are known before video generation and reused during reconstruction. This privileged setup better conditions 4D recovery, allowing model-based object tracking, human motion estimation, and interaction-aware optimization to reconstruct metric 4D human-object interaction (HOI) trajectories with reduced depth ambiguity and morphology mismatch. We retarget the recovered motions to a humanoid robot and train complementary task-general trackers: an object-aware latent adaptor for manipulation and a scene-aware tracker for terrain traversal. GRAIL produces over 20,000 sequences spanning pick-up, object manipulation, sitting, and terrain traversal. Using only GRAIL-generated data, we train egocentric visual policies through a sim-to-real pipeline and deploy them on a Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving 84% real-world success on diverse object pick-up and 90% success on stair-climbing. Code and data will be publicly released.

hSRtOgnkTM.abstract:
Manipulation in submerged settings (e.g., washing dishes, bathing, collecting water samples) is difficult because of the air-water interface. Water makes visual cues unreliable and damages electronics. We learn visuo-tactile policies for this regime by fusing visual observations with tactile and immersion-depth signals from a sensorized waterproof gripper. We train imitation learning transformer policies that use submerged-domain visual augmentations to reduce overfitting to turbidity, reflection- and refraction-related artifacts. 
Across the evaluated submerged manipulation tasks, our full policy achieves a mean success rate of 71%, compared to 41% for the best no-tactile variant. This improvement is especially pronounced under difficult visual conditions, such as floating foam and strong glare. Overall, our results demonstrate combining visual robustness with multimodal tactile sensing improves submerged manipulation. See https://davatar-corl26.github.io/ for details.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision
Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning

PJuQx9kBg5.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
keywords: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming
Deployment-time adaptation of diffusion trajectory planners

uZalcCyrVl.abstract: Teaching humanoids loco-manipulation skills, such as carrying diverse objects, via visual imitation is a promising path toward generalist robots. However, acquiring high-quality, full-body human videos that span a wide variety of object interactions is difficult, leaving too few demonstrations to learn a generalist policy. We propose PRISM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that overcomes this limitation by amplifying a handful of real videos into a large, diverse training set. PRISM first generates hundreds of diverse ``counterfactual'' human–object interaction videos via video-to-video (V2V) generation from a few exemplar real videos. Our contact-anchored real-to-sim pipeline then reconstructs both human and object motions, retargeting this imperfect video data into physically plausible trajectories. The intra-class variability across these counterfactual videos lets us train a single policy that generalizes to unseen objects within each category. We demonstrate the full pipeline by deploying this policy on a real robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Using only onboard depth observations, our humanoid picks up, carries, and drops objects—including boxes, barrels, bins, and balls---across novel instances, sizes, and initial configurations.
keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning
Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

0jY75QYDMn.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations. VLA policies fine-tuned in simulators have so far transferred poorly to humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. We present LEGS (Loco-manipulation via Embodied Gaussian Splatting), a hybrid simulator that composites a mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) over a photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background reconstructed from a handheld scene capture. LEGS uses a procedural motion-primitive generator to synthesize labeled demonstrations at scale without human teleoperation, and a two-stage color calibration that aligns renders to the deployment camera. On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones (psi0, pi0.5, GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only baseline trained on the same motions without the calibrated 3DGS frontend. Because motion is recorded independently of appearance, the same demonstrations can be re-rendered for a target scene and objects at over 15x lower cost than teleoperation. When both the objects and the scene change, a policy trained on LEGS-aug data re-rendered for that target maintains task success, while the teleop baseline fails entirely. Code and videos are available at https://hojjunekim.github.io/legs/.
keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models fine-tuned on LEGS data transfer zero-shot to the real robot and outperform those trained on teleoperation or mesh-only simulation.

NWlhQeCX3L.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge in a purely state-free setting, where a control policy operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable simulation framework that trains visual-inertial, observation-to-command policies entirely from random initialization. By backpropagating through differentiable quadrotor dynamics and smooth task costs, our approach constitutes the first method to learn dynamic narrow-gap traversal without relying on a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using exclusively onboard sensing, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.
keywords: Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control

El4EDBhqCG.abstract: Interactive robot planning requires robots to infer and execute human intentions from natural language instructions that are often ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a powerful interface for clarification, relying on the generative model to drive an multi-turn conversation can introduce systematic failures. We propose a Bayesian framework that treats clarification as an active learning problem over grounded Signal Temporal Logic (STL) task specifications. Our method uses LLMs to initialize candidate formal specifications and translate informative contrasts into natural-language clarification questions, while Bayesian optimization maintains uncertainty estimation over user intent and selects queries that maximize information gain. After convergence, the inferred STL specification is passed to a formal planner to synthesize a verifiable robot trajectory. Across four simulated and real-world task domains, our approach generally achieves higher task satisfaction and requires fewer clarification rounds than LLM baselines, while helping smaller models close the performance gap against larger reasoning models.
keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction
Combination of learning and planning in robotics

Figure 1: Overview of the proposed Bayesian active learning framework.
An LLM proposes candidate specifications with priors, and a grammar VAE embeds them in a latent space where a Gaussian Process (GP) models utility. Queries are sampled by the acquisition function and translated into clarification questions by LLMs. User answers update the GP and the candidates. The final converged specification is decoded and passed to a formal planner for robot execution.

YrNlVJcApO.abstract: Recent world-action models (WAMs) show that co-training policies with future prediction can provide physical priors for action generation. Building on the future-prediction ability of video models, many WAMs generate future videos and recover actions with inverse-dynamics models, or use these predicted videos as goal conditions for action generation. In both cases, the world model is trained mostly on successful demonstrations and has little reason to predict the consequences of bad actions. We introduce CAM, a causal World-Action Model that predicts future video and task progress conditioned on the executed action. This action-conditioned interface allows failure rollouts to supervise action consequences, turning bad actions into valid future targets rather than being discarded. Failure-aware training makes the progress predictor aware of both successful and failed action outcomes, which can optionally be used to score sampled action candidates at inference. Extensive experiments on simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks show that CAM outperforms many existing baselines, improves as failure data are incorporated into training, and reduces success-biased future hallucination under bad actions.
keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Video models and latent world models for robot learning

oX3ErTz3rv.abstract:
Scaling generalist manipulation policies is bottlenecked not by model capacity but by teleoperation cost: covering the full distribution of object placements, orientations, and scene contexts that a deployed robot must handle quickly becomes prohibitive. We argue this bottleneck is largely artificial. Human egocentric demonstrations—plentiful, cheap, and naturally diverse—already encode the visual and physical regularities needed to handle out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations; the missing piece is a recipe that injects this knowledge into a robot-specific action head without re-training the embodiment mapping.                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
Building on LDA-1B, a 1B-parameter latent dynamics-action model pretrained jointly on cross-embodiment robot trajectories and human ego video, we propose a post-training recipe that keeps both data sources alive throughout fine-tuning. Specifically, we co-train with five complementary objectives—policy (P), forward dynamics (FD), inverse dynamics (ID), video generation (VG), and joint action-observation denoising (JD)—routed through embodiment-aware heads. Human ego data participates in FD, ID, VG, and JD but is excluded from policy supervision, so it shapes the shared visual-physical representation while leaving the embodiment-specific action head uncontaminated. We further unfreeze the VLM backbone during post-training, recovering cross-embodiment knowledge that a frozen-VLM recipe otherwise abandons.                                                                                                                        

Across rigorous out-of-distribution evaluations and a suite of long-horizon dexterous manipulation tasks on two robot embodiments, our recipe consistently outperforms robot-only baselines and matches policies trained on substantially more teleoperated data—demonstrating that scarce real-robot demonstrations, combined with abundant egocentric human data, are sufficient for strong generalization.

oX3ErTz3rv.metadataTitle: WAM-TTT: Learning to Adapt World-Action Models from Human Play at Test Time
oX3ErTz3rv.figureCaption: Figure 1: Overview of wam-ttt . Given unlabeled human demonstrations from diverse environments, wam-ttt steers a pretrained World Action Model (WAM) without retargeting, robot actions, or human-side annotations. During deployment, human videos are absorbed into lightweight TTT fast weights through self-supervised video prediction, while the pretrained action model remains frozen. The adapted memory then guides robot execution through the WAM’s shared visual-action dynamics, enabling efficient and reusable steering from human demonstrations.

J5RZyNKq8z.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable alternative to robot data for pretraining, yet models pretrained on such video consistently underperform those pretrained on robot data. We attribute this gap to a missing signal, the active perception behavior in egocentric videos, where humans continuously reposition their viewpoint during manipulation, inducing camera motion that standard pipelines treat as noise. To address this, we present ActiveMimic, a pretraining framework that recovers synchronized camera and wrist trajectories from a single body-worn RGB camera, models camera motion as a viewpoint action, and jointly learns active perception and manipulation from in-the-wild egocentric human video before adapting to a target robot. Empirically, real-world experiments across tasks with diverse active perception demands show that ActiveMimic consistently surpasses baselines pretrained on human video and matches state-of-the-art models pretrained on robot data. Further analysis provides evidence that active perception capability originates from egocentric human video pretraining rather than robot-specific fine-tuning, confirming active perception as the key to unlocking egocentric human video for robot pretraining.

UZnHsKKAAB.abstract:
Robot manipulation has recently achieved significant progress through large-scale learning from teleoperated demonstrations, but collecting such data remains expensive, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale across diverse environments and long-horizon tasks. 
We present SkillWeaver, a scalable framework for autonomous manipulation data generation that combines diverse scene generation, reusable RL-based interaction skills, and VLM-guided hierarchical tree search. Given a task and a generated scene, SkillWeaver adaptively decomposes the task into subgoals, executes contact-rich interactions with closed-loop skills, and collects long-horizon demonstrations with failure recovery and re-planning. In contrast to alternative pipelines that rely on predefined sequencing of hand-designed controllers, grasp predictors, and motion planners, our framework adaptively reasons over object geometries and environment configurations, enabling more flexible and robust behavior generation across diverse tasks and scenes.  We evaluate \model{SkillWeaver} on LIBERO-PRO and a real Franka robot setup, showing that SkillWeaver effectively scales high-quality manipulation data and that large-scale simulation training enables stronger generalization across novel scenarios.
